Stage 1: Sets and statements
HöMa1 · Chapter 1: Sets, Logic and Real Numbers
Axioms speak about “all numbers with a property” and about “if, then.” This stage provides the language for that and a reliable method for proving rules for sets and statements.
Stage 2: Quantifiers and indirect proof
HöMa1 · Chapter 1: Sets, Logic and Real Numbers
All axioms have the form “for all x there is a y.” This stage clarifies how to read and negate such sentences, and how to turn a negation into a proof.
Stage 3: Field axioms
HöMa1 · Chapter 1: Sets, Logic and Real Numbers
Which few rules for plus and times must be assumed so that all other rules of arithmetic become provable?
Stage 4: Order axioms
HöMa1 · Chapter 1: Sets, Logic and Real Numbers
The field axioms say nothing about “greater.” What assumptions lie behind calculating with inequalities?
Stage 5: Mathematical induction, sum and product
HöMa1 · Chapter 1: Sets, Logic and Real Numbers
Statements about all n∈ℕ cannot be proved by trial. This stage provides the method and with it a clean definition of sum, product and power.
Stage 6: The completeness axiom
HöMa1 · Chapter 1: Sets, Logic and Real Numbers
ℚ satisfies all the axioms so far. Yet something is missing: the number whose square is 2. This stage shows that and names the axiom that separates ℝ from ℚ.
Stage 7: Nested intervals and roots
HöMa1 · Chapter 1: Sets, Logic and Real Numbers
The axiom guarantees boundaries. This stage turns that into a construction method and uses it to prove that x²=2 has exactly one positive solution in ℝ.
Stage 8: Distance and absolute value
HöMa1 · Chapter 1: Sets, Logic and Real Numbers
Limits measure how close two numbers lie to each other. For that you need distance and a rule for detours.
Stage 9: Elementary inequalities
HöMa1 · Chapter 1: Sets, Logic and Real Numbers
Often an expression cannot be calculated, only estimated. This stage provides the five standard estimates.

Overview: Complex Numbers
HöMa1 · Chapter 2: Complex Numbers
How a second axis makes x²=-1 solvable and what is lost in the process
Stage 1: Pairs instead of single numbers
HöMa1 · Chapter 2: Complex Numbers
In ℝ, the equation x²=-1 has no solution. This stage builds a larger set of numbers in which the equation is solvable and which contains ℝ unchanged.
Stage 2: The complex plane
HöMa1 · Chapter 2: Complex Numbers
A pair is a point. This stage draws the complex numbers in the plane and shows what addition and multiplication by i mean there.
Stage 3: Reflecting across the real axis
HöMa1 · Chapter 2: Complex Numbers
You cannot yet divide by x+iy. This stage introduces the mirror image of z, which turns any number into a real one by multiplication, and collects the rules of arithmetic.
Stage 4: Division, and what is lost
HöMa1 · Chapter 2: Complex Numbers
Stage 3 provides a real product. This stage turns it into division, shows that ℂ is a field, and explains why the order is missing.
Stage 5: Absolute value and distance
HöMa1 · Chapter 2: Complex Numbers
Complex numbers cannot be ordered, but they can be measured. This stage carries distance and absolute value over from Chapter 1 to the plane and shows which rules survive.
Stage 6: Quadratic equations
HöMa1 · Chapter 2: Complex Numbers
The goal was a solution of x²=-1. This stage shows that ℂ achieves more: Every quadratic equation is solvable there, even with complex coefficients.

When an equation can be solved backward and why every zero splits off a factor
From the ground up: Pairs and intervals
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
When an equation can be solved backward and why every zero splits off a factor
Stage 1: What a function is
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
School presents functions as formulas. That is not enough: A measured relationship has no formula, and the same formula can belong to different functions.
Stage 2: Even, monotonic, bounded
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
The definition says what a function is, but not what it looks like. Three properties save computation: Symmetry halves the work, monotonicity orders the values, boundedness limits them.
Stage 3: Backward: injective, surjective, bijective
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
Going forward, there is exactly one y for each x. Going backward, this guarantee is missing: The equation f(x)=y can have no solution, one, or many.
Stage 4: Combining and inverting
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
Stage 3 says when f(x)=y has exactly one solution. This stage turns the solution into a function.
Stage 5: Polynomials and coefficients
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
The general theory is in place. Now comes the most important family of functions: polynomials, built only from addition and multiplication.
Stage 6: Division with remainder
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
Sum, difference and product of polynomials are again polynomials, but the quotient usually is not.
Stage 7: The Horner scheme
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
For the divisor x-x₀ the division is so regular that a scheme with three rows is enough. At the same time it delivers the value P(x₀) with only n multiplications.
Stage 8: Every zero splits off a linear factor
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
Now the question from the beginning can be answered: Why does a factor belong to every solution of P(x)=0, and how many solutions can there be?
Stage 9: Rational functions and poles
HöMa1 · Chapter 3: Functions and Polynomials
The remainder T/Q from Stage 6 has points where its denominator becomes zero. The function is not defined there.
